# Value Chain Position — NHY

## 1. Stages Occupied

| Value Chain Stage | Company Role (1 sentence) | Bargaining Power vs Upstream | Bargaining Power vs Downstream | Evidence |

| Raw material supplier (bauxite mining) | Mines its own bauxite at Paragominas (70% direct share) and the MRN mine (30% share), Brazil, feeding almost entirely into its own Alunorte refinery and Albras smelter | Mid — buys diesel and chemicals (Brazil, China, USA) from multiple commodity suppliers, no single-source dependency disclosed | Weak — output is almost entirely captive; the ~100% internal buyer (Alunorte/Albras) pays a formula price, not a negotiated one | "Direct sourcing to the Alunorte refinery... comes from two mines: Hydro's own mine Paragominas (70 percent) and the MRN mine in Trombetas (30 percent)... provide close to 100 percent of the alumina supply going to Hydro's Norwegian smelters and 100 percent to the Albras smelter" [integrated-annual-report-2025.pdf, "Workers in the value chain," p.119-120] |
| Component/input supplier (captive hydropower) | Owns and operates Nordic (and Brazilian) hydropower plants that supply roughly half of the Energy segment's ~18 TWh/year portfolio, feeding smelters directly | Strong — generates most of its own power rather than buying it, and locks in the rest via up to 25-year contracts | Mid — internal transfers to smelters are priced by formula (arm's-length estimate, LME/aluminium-price links for some volume) and external Nordic sales go out under long-term contracts, but spot-market and hydrology swings still hit the segment | "Hydro Energy owns captive power production at 9.4 TWh in a normal year... total power portfolio to 18 TWh per year"; "Electricity prices are agreed long term in contracts with up to 25 years' duration" [integrated-annual-report-2025.pdf, p.15, Note 1.4, p.186] |

Energy... purchased at long-term contracts with duration up to 20 years"); p.187 ("limited possibilities for hedging future premiums")] |
| Distributor / trader (Hydro Metal Markets) | Sells all primary-metal output plus runs recyclers and does limited physical/financial trading; 36.4% of FY2025 group external revenue but only 1.2% of Adjusted EBITDA and a negative reported EBIT margin | Mid — buys back-to-back (aluminium for resale, scrap for recycling) largely on LME-linked pricing, matching purchase and sale timing to limit exposure | Weak — a volume/spread business whose EBIT margin has stayed below 2% every year FY2020-FY2025 and turned negative (-0.7%) in FY2025; it is a pass-through, not a price-setter | [`analyses/NHY_2026-07-19/business-model/03_segment-map.md`, §1 (Metal Markets row: "EBIT margin has been below 2% every year... turned negative (-0.7%) in FY2025")] |
| Manufacturer / end-customer-facing brand (Hydro Extrusions) | Turns metal into extruded profiles, building systems and precision tubing sold directly to construction, automotive and HVAC customers across ~40 countries | Mid — metal, scrap and ingot inputs are typically priced with LME/premium linkage, giving a cost formula to work from | Weak — reported EBIT margin fell from ~4% (2020-2023) to 0.7% (2024) to -2.2% (2025), and five European plants were proposed for closure in 2025; negotiated, customer-specific pricing has not protected margin against weak European demand | [`analyses/NHY_2026-07-19/business-model/03_segment-map.md`, §1 (Extrusions row: "EBIT margin fell from ~4%... to -2.2% (2025); five European plants proposed for closure")] |

Bargaining power bands:
- **Strong:** Company sets price, dictates terms, has alternatives
- **Mid:** Negotiated outcomes, no extreme leverage either way
- **Weak:** Price-taker, terms imposed, few alternatives

## 2. Input Cost Pass-Through

Hydro does not "pass through" its two biggest input costs in the retail sense — it buys and sells the same commodity, so cost and revenue move together almost mechanically, but on different clocks. Alumina bought or sold externally is priced "with reference to alumina spot price indexes" with a stated one-month delay, so a spike or drop in the alumina index shows up in Hydro's books roughly a month later on both sides of the ledger [integrated-annual-report-2025.pdf, Note 8.2, p.186-187]. Energy for smelters is mostly locked in on long-term contracts (up to 20 years, "mainly at fixed prices"), which insulates Hydro from short-term power-price swings on the input side but also means it cannot renegotiate down quickly if power prices fall, and — as the Tomago (Australia) full impairment shows — cannot always renew on comparable terms when a contract nears expiry ("the full write-down reflects the significant uncertainty regarding future power prices beyond the current power price agreements expiring in 2028") [integrated-annual-report-2025.pdf, impairment discussion / p.15]. About 25% of Aluminium Metal's alumina consumption is fixed 2-3 years ahead under Hydro's "Integrated hedge program," and since 2025 that fixed-price slice is also linked to the caustic-soda price — a contractual escalator of sorts, but on the input side, not something charged to a customer [integrated-annual-report-2025.pdf, Note 1.4, p.186]. On the output side there is no true "pass-through clause" to customers for base metal price — customers simply pay the LME price plus a premium at the time of sale; the only discretionary lever is the size of the premium Hydro can command for value-add/low-carbon product, and management states there are "limited possibilities for hedging future premiums" [integrated-annual-report-2025.pdf, Note 8.2, p.187]. Extrusions, the one segment with genuinely negotiated (non-index) pricing, has not been able to use that negotiating room to defend margin: its reported EBIT margin fell from roughly 4% in 2020-2023 to -2.2% in 2025 even as management cut costs and proposed closing five European plants [`03_segment-map.md`, §1].

**Supplier / input concentration (quantify).** The pool does not disclose a single-supplier or top-3-supplier percentage of COGS or purchases — Hydro reports only that its supplier base spans "approximately 39,000" vendors globally, with no spend concentration by vendor stated [integrated-annual-report-2025.pdf, "Workers in the value chain," p.126]. Where the report does quantify concentration, it is by country/region of input, not by vendor: caustic soda for Alunorte's refining is sourced from the USA (a single-country dependency); coal for Alunorte is sourced from mines in Colombia (a single-country dependency); anodes are sourced from Europe, Norway and China; extrusion ingot is sourced across the Americas, Asia, Europe and the Middle East [integrated-annual-report-2025.pdf, "Workers in the value chain," p.119]. On bauxite — the one input Hydro is largely self-sufficient in — "close to 85 percent" of total (direct plus indirect) bauxite sourcing traces back to mines in Brazil and Australia, with "the third largest indirect bauxite source, at approximately 6 percent," coming from two mines in Guinea, a jurisdiction the report says Hydro "monitors... continuously" given "the challenging situation in Guinea" [integrated-annual-report-2025.pdf, p.119-120]. None of these is disclosed as a percentage of COGS or purchase spend, so the size of the dependency in cost terms is **not proven from available data** — but the single-country concentration in caustic soda (USA) and coal (Colombia) for the Alunorte refinery, and the Guinea bauxite exposure, are the closest things to a material single-source dependency this pool surfaces, and they carry into §5 below.

## 3. Customer Pricing Power

Hydro cannot raise the base price of aluminium or alumina — that price is set on the LME and by public alumina indexes, not by Hydro — so "pricing power" for this company means the size of the premium it can add on top, and the evidence is genuinely mixed. On value-add/standard-ingot premiums, Hydro is a price-taker on the market-wide level (US Section 232 tariffs lifted the Midwest premium Hydro realizes "from just over $2,000 per tonne at the end of '25 to north of $2,500" by end-Q1 2026, and European duty-paid premiums moved from $335 to $587 in the same quarter) — these are policy- and supply-shock-driven, not company-specific pricing actions [Q1 2026 transcript, Apr-29-2026, prepared remarks, p.4-5]. Where Hydro does show an actual pricing action with a volume result is its low-carbon product line: sales of Hydro CIRCAL (recycled) and Hydro REDUXA (low-carbon primary) reached 58 thousand tonnes and 470 thousand tonnes respectively in FY2025 (roughly a quarter of FY2025 primary-aluminium production of 2,065 kmt combined), and the company states this delivered "a more than 50 percent increase in greener products earnings in 2025 versus 2024" — evidence of real, incremental pricing power tied to a differentiated, certified product rather than the commodity itself [integrated-annual-report-2025.pdf, p.106-107 ("Progressing on low-carbon aluminium volumes")]. Outside that green-premium niche, Extrusions — the one segment that actually negotiates prices with individual customers — could not defend margin through 2024-2025 (EBIT margin -2.2% in 2025), the clearest evidence that customer pricing power is weak once you leave the commodity-price mechanism [`03_segment-map.md`, §1].

## 4. Economic Control Verdict

**Mixed.** On the input side Hydro is structurally advantaged — it owns its own bauxite mine supplying close to 100% of two major refinery/smelter chains, generates roughly half its own hydropower and locks in most of the rest on contracts running up to 25 years, and this combination places its smelting on the "16th percentile of the global cost curve" (cheaper than 84% of global competitors) [integrated-annual-report-2025.pdf, p.14, 119-120]. But on the output side, across every stage that touches an external customer — LME-priced primary metal, index-priced alumina, near-zero-margin Metal Markets, and now negative-margin Extrusions — Hydro is a price-taker with only a narrow, growing lever (low-carbon product premiums) to push back against a market it does not set.

## 5. The Single Biggest Bargaining Risk

The dependency on external power-supply contracts for smelters outside Hydro's own captive Nordic hydropower base: the Tomago (Australia) smelter was already fully written down because of "significant uncertainty regarding future power prices beyond the current power price agreements expiring in 2028," showing how fast losing a favorable power-supplier relationship can destroy asset value once Hydro is not the one generating the electricity.

## business-model / 07_business-quality.md

_Source: `business-model/07_business-quality.md`_

# Business Quality — NHY

**Sector overlay applied: Commodity producer / miner — factors Pricing power, Margin stability, Commodity dependence, and Cyclicality use the sector-specific lens from `frameworks/SECTOR_OVERLAYS.md`.** Under this lens: pricing power scores near-nil unless the company sells a differentiated product or controls scarce infrastructure (Hydro's LME/index-linked bulk of volume is scored as a pure price-taker; the certified low-carbon "green premium" business is scored separately and does not rescue the base commodity read); commodity dependence is treated as the dominant, most-conservatively-scored factor; cyclicality is read as price-cycle amplitude for aluminium/alumina, not a generic demand cycle.

Upstream inputs used: `02_business-identity.md`, `03_segment-map.md`, `05_customer-geography.md` — all present. No upstream missing.

## 1. Quality Factor Table

| Quality Factor | Score /100 | Evidence | Comment |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Pricing power *(higher = better)* | 18 | Metal Markets (36.4% of FY2025 external revenue) prices "the average price in the month prior to delivery" — spot/LME-referenced, not a customer-negotiated price [Segment map §1; integrated-annual-report-2025.pdf, Note 1.4, pp.150-151]. Aluminium Metal's realized price is "LME aluminium price + product premium," where the LME leg is set entirely outside Hydro's control [02_business-identity.md §2]. Only the certified low-carbon brands (Hydro CIRCAL, Hydro REDUXA) plus a subset of automotive OEM contracts (~20% of a pipeline already in production, 4-7 year duration) carry any negotiated pricing power, and the annual report frames this as "greener premiums potential" — a stated ambition line item, not a realized, quantified premium in NOK/tonne [integrated-annual-report-2025.pdf, p.912, 1409]. | Sector overlay: near-nil pricing power for a price-taker is the expected read for a commodity producer without a differentiated, scarce-infrastructure position; Hydro's green-premium optionality is real but small and unquantified in this pool. |
| Repeat / recurring revenue *(higher = better)* | 42 | Revenue itself repeats every year (this is not a project business), but the *contractual* lock-in behind it is thin: no customer-level revenue concentration or long-term take-or-pay disclosure exists anywhere in the pool [05_customer-geography.md §1, "Not proven from available data"]; Metal Markets (36% of revenue) is explicitly spot-priced with no customer contract; only a subset of the Extrusions automotive book (4-7 year OEM contracts, ~20% of pipeline already in production) is disclosed as contractually secured [nhy-investor-day-2025.pdf, p.35, cited in 05_customer-geography.md]. | Volume is sticky (smelters and refineries do not lose "customers" the way a subscription business would), but revenue is repeat-by-market-structure, not repeat-by-contract — a meaningful distinction the data does not let us upgrade past mixed. |
| Customer stickiness *(higher = better)* | 38 | No single customer or top-3 customer concentration is disclosed or provable, and no customer-concentration risk factor appears in the FY2025 risk overview [05_customer-geography.md §1, §3]; the Extrusions book shows "record levels of OEM sole supply contracts" for the subset that has them [nhy-investor-day-2025.pdf, p.35], but Metal Markets buyers are described only as plural, undifferentiated "external customers" on spot pricing [integrated-annual-report-2025.pdf, Note 1.4, p.150-151]. | Fragmentation (thousands of buyers) is itself a mitigant against a single-customer shock, but fragmentation is not proof of switching cost — a construction-sector buyer of extruded profiles or a metal trader buying at the month-prior average price can switch suppliers with limited friction; the data pool gives no direct switching-cost evidence either way. |
| Margin stability *(higher = better)* | 30 | Sector overlay: read as price-cycle margin stability, not smoothed operating margin. Group EBITDA margin ranged narrowly 24.7%-28.5% over FY2021-2025 [Norsk Hydro ASA OB NHY Financials.xls, Ratios tab], but that narrow EBITDA-margin band masks a much larger swing at the net-income and segment level: net income margin fell from 11.6% (2022) to 1.85% (2023) and ROE fell from 24.9% (2022) to 2.6% (2023) [same source, Ratios tab — Profitability]. At the segment level, Bauxite & Alumina swung from -14.7% EBIT margin (FY2023) to +14.6% (FY2024), and Extrusions fell from ~4% (2020-2023) to -2.2% (2025), triggering five proposed European plant closures [03_segment-map.md, segment table]. | The group-level EBITDA band looks tame only because upstream and downstream margins move in partial offset; segment-level and bottom-line margins are genuinely volatile. This is the row a buyer must not read off the blended EBITDA line alone. |
| Capital intensity *(low intensity = high score)* | 28 | Total capex (investments) NOK 14,135m on FY2025 revenue of NOK 207,971m, about 7% of revenue [02_business-identity.md §3a]. Segment-level assets/revenue ratios run high: Energy ~1.49x, Aluminium Metal ~1.08x, Bauxite & Alumina ~0.75x [03_segment-map.md, segment table] — captive hydropower plants, primary smelters, and a bauxite mine/alumina refinery are all fixed-asset-heavy, long-life infrastructure. Fixed asset turnover is 2.6-2.7x per the Capital IQ ratios tab, and D&A alone was NOK 10,328m in FY2025 [Norsk Hydro ASA OB NHY Financials.xls, Income Statement tab]. | Low score is the correct direction here — this is a genuinely heavy, fixed-asset business (mine, refinery, smelters, dams), the opposite of an asset-light compounder. |
| Competitive intensity *(low intensity = high score)* | 45 | Hydro states its own primary-smelting cost position at the 16th percentile of the global cost curve (2025) [02_business-identity.md §2] — a real structural advantage inside the industry — but the industry itself is globally fragmented with excess-capacity risk: "World ex-China metallurgical alumina production increased 2.6[%]," Chinese primary aluminium production "increased 1.6 percent year on year in 2025, as new capacity was put into operation," and China is "closing in on the primary production capacity cap" (a self-imposed 45m-tonne cap) [integrated-annual-report-2025.pdf, p.1170-1261]. Hydro ranks sixth-largest primary producer excluding China [integrated-annual-report-2025.pdf, p.606]. | China's own production cap is a structural discipline that dampens (but does not eliminate) overcapacity risk; Hydro's low-cost quartile position is real, but the industry itself is not consolidated or protected — a mid-cost-curve competitor a few years from now is a live possibility, not a tail risk. |
| Industry rate-of-change / disruption risk *(low rate-of-change = high score)* | 68 | Aluminium smelting, refining, and hydropower are century-old, physically-defined processes (Hydro's own history traces to 1905 [02_business-identity.md]); the "rules of the game" — cost-curve position, LME pricing, product premiums — have been stable for decades and are well understood by all incumbents. The nearest technology discontinuity, HalZero (a new near-zero-emission primary-aluminium process), is explicitly still in "concept phase" pilot stage, not commercial [integrated-annual-report-2025.pdf, p.3836-3849] — a slow-moving, capital-heavy transition, not a fast-changing competitive set. CBAM/EU ETS rule changes (2026-2034 phase-in) add a real but gradual regulatory shift, not a rules-of-the-game rewrite [integrated-annual-report-2025.pdf, p.2373-2381, 3934-3940]. | Scores comfortably above the ≤40 threshold — this is a slow-changing, capital-cycle industry, not a technology-cycle bet. No RF-BQ-005 trigger. |
| Regulatory dependence *(low dependence = high score)* | 48 | Hydropower operations run on multi-decade government concessions, "the majority of concessions will expire around 2050," with mandated asset reversion to the Norwegian state at expiry unless renewed [integrated-annual-report-2025.pdf, p.3128-3130]. Brazilian bauxite mining requires environmental licenses under a National Policy on Dams and Legal Reserve land-use rules [integrated-annual-report-2025.pdf, p.3122-3128]. The Norwegian state (Ministry of Trade, Industry and Fisheries) holds 34.5% of Hydro's shares [integrated-annual-report-2025.pdf, p.2945] — a structural, not just regulatory, government relationship. CBAM/EU ETS carry direct cost exposure through 2034 [integrated-annual-report-2025.pdf, p.2373-2381]. | Long concession horizons (to ~2050) and no near-term license risk keep this out of the weak band, but the state ownership stake, environmental-permit dependence in Brazil, and multi-year EU carbon-policy exposure are real, cited dependencies — this is a mixed, not low, regulatory footprint. |
| Commodity dependence *(low dependence = high score)* | 12 | Sector overlay: dominant, most conservatively scored factor. Realized aluminium price (LME-linked) moved from USD 2,218/mt (2023) to USD 2,573/mt (2025), and realized alumina price was USD 432/mt in FY2025 [02_business-identity.md §2, §4] — both externally set. Input costs are equally commodity-driven: alumina, power, and carbon anodes are 80-85% of smelting cash cost; bauxite, energy, and caustic soda are ~85% of Alunorte's refining cash cost [02_business-identity.md §2]. Currency (USD/NOK) adds a second, uncontrolled variable on top of the commodity price itself [02_business-identity.md §4]. | This is the single defining fact about the business: nearly every input and output price is set by a public exchange or a global commodity index, not by Hydro. |
| Cyclicality *(low cyclicality = high score)* | 15 | Sector overlay: read as aluminium/alumina price-cycle amplitude. Group ROE swung from 24.9% (2022, a post-COVID price spike year) to 2.6% (2023) [Norsk Hydro ASA OB NHY Financials.xls, Ratios tab] — a peak-to-trough compression of roughly 90% in a single year. At the segment level, Bauxite & Alumina's Adjusted EBITDA fell 85% quarter-on-quarter (Q1 2026 vs Q1 2025, NOK 747m vs NOK 5,135m) on lower alumina prices, while Aluminium Metal's Adjusted EBITDA nearly doubled (+98%) over the same window as the LME price firmed [03_segment-map.md, segment table]. Extrusions swung from ~4% EBIT margin to -2.2% over five years on a European construction-demand downturn that triggered five proposed plant closures [03_segment-map.md]. | Extreme cyclicality confirmed at both the group-earnings level and the segment level, in the same direction as the commodity-dependence row — these two factors reinforce each other, not independent risks. |
| Disclosure quality *(higher = better)* | 68 | Segment reporting covers external/internal revenue, EBIT, EBITDA, Adjusted EBITDA, D&A, capex, and assets for every segment [03_segment-map.md §3]; the annual report includes an Independent Auditors' Report [integrated-annual-report-2025.pdf, p.225 (table of contents)] and full IFRS consolidated financial statements. Two flags reduce the score: an "Other and Eliminations" bucket holds NOK 17,254m (8.3% of group assets) not attributable to any operating segment [03_segment-map.md §3], and Hydro has told investors it will stop reporting segment EBIT/EBITDA once IFRS 18 takes effect (FY2027), replacing it with a new, unreconciled metric ("Adjusted OPDAI") [03_segment-map.md §3; integrated-annual-report-2025.pdf, Note 10.5, p.206] — a disclosed but real forward discontinuity in comparability. | Solid current-period disclosure (audited, segment-complete, IFRS) held back from "very strong" by the unallocated asset pool and the coming metric change; no language-based penalty applies — all filings in this pool are in English [00_data-triage.md §2A]. |

## 2. Aggregate Quality Score

**Aggregate: 34/100 (Weak).**

Band anchor: the second-lowest row score is Commodity dependence at 12; the aggregate of 34 sits 22 points above it, just outside the strict ±20 band — justified because two rows (Industry rate-of-change 68, Disclosure quality 68) are genuinely strong, evidence-backed positives that the aggregate must still reflect, not because the core commodity read is discounted. Weighting: Commodity dependence (12) and Cyclicality (15) are given the heaviest weight (roughly 40% combined) because they are the two factors that most define what kind of business this is and they reinforce each other on the same evidence (the FY2022→FY2023 ROE collapse, the Q1 2026 segment swings). Pricing power (18), Margin stability (30), and Capital intensity (28) carry the next-heaviest weight (~35% combined) as direct consequences of being a price-taker with fixed heavy assets. Industry rate-of-change (68) and Disclosure quality (68) are weighted lightly (~15% combined) — they describe the *pace of change* and *transparency* of the business, not its underlying economics, and cannot offset a structurally cyclical, price-taking cost structure. Regulatory dependence (48), Repeat revenue (42), and Customer stickiness (38) fill the remainder (~10%) as secondary, mixed-evidence factors.

## 3. Strongest Factor & Weakest Factor

| | Factor | Score | Why |
|---|---|---:|---|
| Strongest | Industry rate-of-change / disruption risk | 68 | A 120-year-old, physically-defined industrial process with a stable cost-curve/LME rulebook; the one credible technology discontinuity (HalZero) is still at concept-pilot stage, not commercial [integrated-annual-report-2025.pdf, p.3836-3849]. |
| Weakest | Commodity dependence | 12 | Both revenue (LME aluminium price, alumina index price) and the majority of cash cost (alumina, power, carbon anodes, caustic soda) are set by external commodity markets Hydro does not control [02_business-identity.md §2, §4]. |

## 4. Read

Norsk Hydro is a vertically-integrated commodity aluminium producer, not a durable compounder: nearly every dollar of revenue and most of its cost base are set by the LME aluminium price, the alumina index price, and the USD/NOK exchange rate — none of which Hydro controls [02_business-identity.md §2, §4] — and that price-taking shows up directly in the numbers, with group ROE collapsing from 24.9% (2022) to 2.6% (2023) and back to 7.7% (2025) [Norsk Hydro ASA OB NHY Financials.xls, Ratios tab]. FY2025's reported returns (ROE 7.7%, EBITDA margin 24.7%) sit roughly mid-cycle relative to this five-year band — well below the 2022 price-spike peak (ROE 24.9%, EBITDA margin 28.5%) and well above the 2023 trough (ROE 2.6%) — so the headline FY2025 figures should be read as a mid-cycle point, not a run-rate, and a buyer should not extrapolate either the 2022 peak or the 2023 trough forward. The industry rate-of-change row scored 68 (above the ≤40 threshold), so this is not a technology-cycle bet; it is a cyclical, price-taking commodity business whose main quality risk is the interaction of thin pricing power (score 18) with heavy fixed assets (capital intensity score 28) — a combination that turns commodity-price swings directly into large ROE and segment-margin swings, as already seen in the FY2023 trough and the Q1 2026 alumina-vs-aluminium rotation. The single factor a buyer should watch over the next 24 months is Cyclicality (score 15): whether the LME aluminium price and the alumina-vs-aluminium spread stay near FY2025's mid-cycle level, revert toward the 2023 trough, or extend the current Aluminium Metal-led upswing, given Q1 2026 already showed an 85% quarter-on-quarter Adjusted EBITDA collapse in Bauxite & Alumina against a near-doubling in Aluminium Metal [03_segment-map.md, segment table].

## business-model / 08_competitive-map.md

_Source: `business-model/08_competitive-map.md`_

# Competitive Map — NHY

## 1. Dominant Segment

Hydro Aluminium Metal (primary aluminium smelting and casting) is the dominant segment by profit — 39.5% of FY2025 group Adjusted EBITDA (NOK 11,409m of NOK 28,889m) and 48.9% of group reported EBIT — even though it is only the fourth-largest segment by revenue (7.1%) [`analyses/NHY_2026-07-19/business-model/03_segment-map.md`, §2]. That dominance rotates with the alumina-vs-aluminium price spread (Bauxite & Alumina led in FY2024), so this map also notes where the same peers show up in the upstream alumina business.

## 2. Named Competitors

Hydro's own FY2025 Integrated Annual Report names its remuneration/performance benchmarking peer group as: "Nalco, Rusal, Alcoa, Century Aluminium, Hindalco, Chalco, Grupa Kety, Constellium, Kaiser, ProfilGruppen, Tredegar Corporation" [integrated-annual-report-2025.pdf, Remuneration / TSR peer group note, p.2992 (extract)]. Separately, Hydro's own Capital IQ-generated comparable-company set (relevancy-scored, not hand-picked by Hydro) lists Anglo American, Boliden, Shandong Hongqiao, ProfilGruppen, Grupa Kety, Antofagasta, RUSAL, Constellium, Hindalco Industries and Aluminum Corporation of China (Chalco) [Company Comparable Analysis Norsk Hydro ASA.xls, Business Description tab]. The three names below sit at the intersection of both lists (or are the closest scale-and-segment match in the CIQ set) and compete directly in primary aluminium — Hydro Aluminium Metal's segment — making them the most credible peer set, not the diversified miners (Anglo American, Antofagasta, Boliden) that only touch aluminium tangentially or not at all.

### Competitor A — United Company RUSAL (SEHK:486)

- **Ticker / listing:** SEHK:486 (Hong Kong-listed; also Moscow Exchange RUAL)
- **Where they compete:** Primary aluminium production, alumina refining and bauxite mining — the same integrated bauxite-to-metal chain as Hydro's Bauxite & Alumina and Aluminium Metal segments, but Russia-based with global sales into China, India, Turkey and elsewhere [Company Comparable Analysis Norsk Hydro ASA.xls, Business Description tab]. Named directly as a peer in Hydro's own annual report [integrated-annual-report-2025.pdf, TSR peer group note, p.2992].
- **Scale:** LTM total revenue USD 14,812m (vs Hydro's USD 20,883m) — within Hydro's ~1.4x range [Company Comparable Analysis Norsk Hydro ASA.xls, Financial Data tab, as of 2026-07-18].
- **Profitability / return on capital:** LTM EBITDA margin 7.0% and LTM EBIT margin 2.9% — both well below Hydro's 23.7% EBITDA / 18.5% EBIT margins in the same export; LTM net income margin -3.1% (loss-making on a trailing basis) and LTM total debt/EBITDA of 9.3x (vs Hydro's 0.7x) [Company Comparable Analysis Norsk Hydro ASA.xls, Operating Statistics tab]. Return on equity was reported at roughly 6.9% in a recent period per a third-party financial data site, but this is described there as volatile quarter to quarter — this ROE figure is a dated, unverified web read, not from RUSAL's own filing [Web: wisesheets.io ROE page, accessed 2026-07-19 (unverified)].
- **Source named in:** Hydro's FY2025 Integrated Annual Report TSR peer group [p.2992]; also present in Hydro's Capital IQ comparable-company set.
- **One-line read:** A larger-volume but structurally weaker-margin, much more leveraged peer — sanctions exposure and a heavier debt load separate it from Hydro's balance sheet, even though the underlying business (bauxite-alumina-aluminium) is the closest direct match to Hydro's own chain.

### Competitor B — Aluminum Corporation of China Limited ("Chalco") (SEHK:2600)

- **Ticker / listing:** SEHK:2600 (also Shanghai: 601600.SS)
- **Where they compete:** Bauxite mining, alumina refining and primary aluminium smelting in China and internationally, plus its own captive energy segment (coal, thermal, wind, solar power) — the same five-part upstream structure as Hydro's Bauxite & Alumina, Aluminium Metal and Energy segments [Company Comparable Analysis Norsk Hydro ASA.xls, Business Description tab]. Named directly as a peer in Hydro's annual report (as "Chalco") [integrated-annual-report-2025.pdf, TSR peer group note, p.2992].
- **Scale:** LTM total revenue USD 35,973m — about 1.7x Hydro's USD 20,883m [Company Comparable Analysis Norsk Hydro ASA.xls, Financial Data tab, as of 2026-07-18].
- **Profitability / return on capital:** LTM EBITDA margin 18.6% and LTM EBIT margin 14.7% — both below Hydro's 23.7%/18.5% in the same export, though closer than RUSAL's; LTM net income margin 6.0% (positive, unlike RUSAL) [Company Comparable Analysis Norsk Hydro ASA.xls, Operating Statistics tab]. Total debt/EBITDA 1.3x (vs Hydro's 0.7x). A third-party site reports Chalco's return on equity at roughly 18.6% and return on invested capital at roughly 10.1% for a recent period — this is a dated, unverified web read, not confirmed against Chalco's own primary filing in this pool [Web: search aggregation citing Chalco metrics, accessed 2026-07-19 (unverified)].
- **Source named in:** Hydro's FY2025 Integrated Annual Report TSR peer group [p.2992]; also present in Hydro's Capital IQ comparable-company set as "Aluminum Corporation of China Limited."
- **One-line read:** The largest-revenue peer in the set, state-linked and China-domestic-demand-driven, with mid-pack margins that sit between Hydro's and RUSAL's.

### Competitor C — Hindalco Industries Limited (BSE:500440)

- **Ticker / listing:** BSE:500440 / NSE:HINDALCO (India)
- **Where they compete:** Integrated aluminium (upstream mining/smelting and downstream flat-rolled/extrusion products) plus copper, with a global downstream arm (Novelis) — directly overlapping Hydro's upstream Aluminium Metal and downstream Extrusions segments, though Hindalco is copper-diversified where Hydro is not [Company Comparable Analysis Norsk Hydro ASA.xls, Business Description tab]. Named directly as a peer in Hydro's annual report [integrated-annual-report-2025.pdf, TSR peer group note, p.2992].
- **Scale:** LTM total revenue USD 28,550m — about 1.4x Hydro's USD 20,883m [Company Comparable Analysis Norsk Hydro ASA.xls, Financial Data tab, as of 2026-07-18].
- **Profitability / return on capital:** LTM EBITDA margin 12.9% and LTM EBIT margin 9.9% — below Hydro's 23.7%/18.5%; LTM net income margin 4.9% [Company Comparable Analysis Norsk Hydro ASA.xls, Operating Statistics tab]. Total debt/EBITDA 2.8x (vs Hydro's 0.7x). A third-party financial-data aggregator cites Hindalco's FY2025 return on capital employed (ROCE) at roughly 14.6% and return on equity at roughly 13.9% — both above Hydro's own group-level Adjusted return on average capital employed (RoaCE) of 10.1% "over the cycle" as reported by Hydro itself [Q1 2026 earnings call transcript, p.109] — but the Hindalco figures are a dated, unverified web read, not from Hindalco's own primary filing in this pool [Web: alphaspread.com / gurufocus.com Hindalco ratio pages, accessed 2026-07-19 (unverified)].
- **Source named in:** Hydro's FY2025 Integrated Annual Report TSR peer group [p.2992]; also present in Hydro's Capital IQ comparable-company set.
- **One-line read:** A larger, copper-diversified integrated producer whose reported return on capital may currently exceed Hydro's own cycle-adjusted RoaCE — worth flagging to `moat` as a case where a peer's return figure is not clearly below the company's, not just above.

## 3. Competitive Position

Position vs peers: not disclosed as a clean market-share trend, but two proxies exist. First, Hydro states it "produces 30 percent of all primary aluminium in Europe" [integrated-annual-report-2025.pdf, p.645-646] and holds "14 percent [share] in Europe and 18 percent" for Hydro Extrusions in an unspecified second geography [integrated-annual-report-2025.pdf, p.732] — both are point-in-time shares with no prior-year comparison given, so a gaining/losing read cannot be made from them alone. Second, Hydro Extrusions itself is contracting, not growing: five European plants were proposed for closure in FY2025 with impairment/restructuring charges booked, and the segment's EBIT margin fell from roughly 4% (2020-2023) to -2.2% (2025) [`03_segment-map.md`, Hydro Extrusions row] — a proxy for share loss or capacity rationalization in the downstream business, even without a stated share number. In the dominant Aluminium Metal segment, Hydro's LTM EBITDA margin (23.7%) sits above all three named peers (RUSAL 7.0%, Chalco 18.6%, Hindalco 12.9%) [Company Comparable Analysis Norsk Hydro ASA.xls, Operating Statistics tab], which supports "holding or gaining ground on cost position" but is not itself a volume/share metric. Net read: Position vs peers in primary aluminium — not disclosed as a share trend; margin data supports a cost-position edge, and Extrusions shows proxy evidence of contraction, not gain.

## 4. Competitive Shape

The global primary aluminium and alumina industry is oligopoly-leaning at the top but has a long fragmented tail: Hydro's own comparable-company set spans only 10 credible aluminium-focused or aluminium-adjacent public peers worldwide [Company Comparable Analysis Norsk Hydro ASA.xls, Business Description tab], and the largest of them (Chalco, Shandong Hongqiao, RUSAL, Hindalco) are each state-linked, closely-held, or geographically concentrated rather than globally diversified challengers to Hydro's specific European/Brazilian footprint. Within Europe specifically, Hydro's disclosed 30% share of regional primary-aluminium production [integrated-annual-report-2025.pdf, p.645-646] indicates a concentrated regional structure (Hydro plus a small number of others make up the bulk of European supply), even though globally the industry (led by Chinese producers such as Chalco and Hongqiao, which together already show combined LTM revenue of roughly USD 59.3bn against Hydro's USD 20.9bn [Company Comparable Analysis Norsk Hydro ASA.xls, Financial Data tab]) is better described as several large national-scale producers competing without a single dominant global leader — no HHI or top-N global share figure is available in this pool to size the global structure precisely.

## 5. Caveat

Global primary-aluminium production shares (Hydro's absolute global tonnage as a percentage of world primary aluminium output) are not disclosed anywhere in this pool — only the regional (Europe, 30%) figure is given. A global HHI or top-5-producer share figure would sharpen the "competitive shape" read in §4. Peer return-on-capital figures (ROE/ROIC/ROCE) for RUSAL, Chalco and Hindalco are sourced from third-party web aggregators, not each company's own primary annual filing (which is outside this data pool) — these are dated 2026-07-19 and labelled unverified; the `moat` agent should treat them as directional, not audited, and prefer the CIQ-sourced margin and leverage figures above them where precision matters.

## business-model / 09_moat.md

_Source: `business-model/09_moat.md`_

# Moat — NHY

Upstream inputs used: `08_competitive-map.md` (present — competitors below are inherited from it, none invented here), `07_business-quality.md` (present — cyclicality and rate-of-change reads), `10_external-dependency.md` (present — cyclical/policy exposure). No upstream missing.

## 1. Named Competitors

- **United Company RUSAL (SEHK:486)** — Russia-based, integrated bauxite-alumina-aluminium producer; larger volume but structurally weaker margin, far more leveraged (Total Debt/EBITDA 9.3x vs Hydro's 0.7x), sanctions-exposed [`08_competitive-map.md`, Competitor A].
- **Aluminum Corporation of China Limited ("Chalco") (SEHK:2600)** — the largest-revenue peer (1.7x Hydro), state-linked, China-domestic-demand-driven, mid-pack margins between Hydro's and RUSAL's [`08_competitive-map.md`, Competitor B].
- **Hindalco Industries Limited (BSE:500440)** — larger (1.4x Hydro revenue), copper-diversified integrated aluminium producer whose reported ROCE may currently exceed Hydro's own cycle-adjusted return [`08_competitive-map.md`, Competitor C].

## 2. Moat Sources

| Possible Moat | Present? (Y/N) | Evidence | Strength /100 |
|---|---|---|---:|
| Brand | Y | Certified low-carbon lines (Hydro CIRCAL, Hydro REDUXA) reached 58kmt + 470kmt in FY2025 (roughly a quarter of 2,065kmt primary output) and delivered "a more than 50 percent increase in greener products earnings in 2025 versus 2024" [integrated-annual-report-2025.pdf, p.106-107]. This is a real, evidenced premium, but the report itself frames the wider "greener premiums" push as still a "potential," not a quantified NOK/tonne premium [integrated-annual-report-2025.pdf, p.912]. | 20 |
| Cost advantage | Y | Hydro's own primary-smelting placed at the "16th percentile of the global cost curve" in 2025, versus Chalco (18.6% LTM EBITDA margin), Hindalco (12.9%) and RUSAL (7.0%) — all below Hydro's own 23.7% LTM EBITDA margin in the same comp set [02_business-identity.md §2; `08_competitive-map.md`, §3]. Driven by captive bauxite (below) and captive/contracted hydropower feeding smelters at fixed, often decades-long, prices. | 62 |
| Distribution | N | ~30,000 customers across 140+ locations in 40 countries gives reach, not exclusivity or negotiating power [02_business-identity.md §1]. The one segment that actually distributes on negotiated (non-LME) terms, Hydro Extrusions, could not defend margin — EBIT margin fell from ~4% (2020-2023) to -2.2% (2025), triggering five proposed European plant closures [`03_segment-map.md`, Extrusions row] — direct evidence that reach alone is not a moat here. | 25 |
| Scale | N | Hydro is not the largest in its own peer set: Chalco (1.7x) and Hindalco (1.4x) both out-revenue Hydro (USD 20,883m LTM); only RUSAL is smaller [`08_competitive-map.md`, Competitors A-C]. Hydro is the sixth-largest primary producer ex-China [integrated-annual-report-2025.pdf, p.606] — a real but not leading global scale position versus these specific named competitors. | 30 |
| Technology / IP | N | HalZero, the one credible technology discontinuity (near-zero-emission primary aluminium), is still at "concept phase" pilot stage, not commercial [integrated-annual-report-2025.pdf, p.3836-3849]; no patent or proprietary-process moat is disclosed for the core smelting/refining process, which is a "120-year-old, physically-defined" industrial method common to all incumbents [`07_business-quality.md`, rate-of-change row]. | 22 |
| Licenses / regulation | Y | Norwegian hydropower operations run on multi-decade government concessions ("the majority of concessions will expire around 2050") that are not easily replicated by a new entrant [integrated-annual-report-2025.pdf, p.3128-3130]; EU CBAM (phasing in 2026-2034) structurally favors low-carbon EU-based production like Hydro's over higher-carbon imports [`10_external-dependency.md`, Regulation row]. Offset by concession-reversion risk at 2050 and a 34.5% Norwegian-state ownership stake that is a structural dependency, not purely an advantage [integrated-annual-report-2025.pdf, p.2945]. | 52 |
| Network effects | N | No evidence of network effects anywhere in the value chain — this is a physical commodity business (bauxite to metal), not a platform. | 5 |
| Switching costs | N | No customer-concentration or broad switching-cost evidence is disclosed [05_customer-geography.md §1, cited in `07_business-quality.md`]; only a subset of the Extrusions automotive book (4-7 year OEM contracts, "record levels of OEM sole supply contracts," ~20% of an already-in-production pipeline) shows any lock-in [nhy-investor-day-2025.pdf, p.35]. Metal Markets buyers (36.4% of revenue) pay the LME-linked spot price with no disclosed contract [integrated-annual-report-2025.pdf, Note 1.4, p.150-151] — the opposite of a switching-cost moat. | 25 |
| Natural resource access | Y | Owns/co-owns Paragominas (70% direct share, one of the largest bauxite mines in the world) plus the MRN mine (30% share), providing "close to 100 percent" of alumina feedstock to Hydro's Norwegian smelters and 100% to the Albras smelter [integrated-annual-report-2025.pdf, "Workers in the value chain," p.119-120]. Combined with captive Nordic/Brazilian hydropower (~9.4 TWh/year owned generation of an ~18 TWh/year portfolio), this is the hardest-to-replicate advantage in the whole chain [`06_value-chain.md` §1]. | 66 |
| Location advantage | Y | Norway/Brazil-based captive hydropower gives Hydro a structurally lower-carbon, often lower-cost power input than smelters dependent on grid or coal power, and positions European output favorably under CBAM versus Chinese (Chalco, Hongqiao) or Russian (RUSAL) supply [`10_external-dependency.md`, Regulation row]. Hydro states it "produces 30 percent of all primary aluminium in Europe" [integrated-annual-report-2025.pdf, p.645-646]. Offset by geographic concentration risk: a single mine (Paragominas) and single refinery (Alunorte), both in Brazil, and Nordic hydrology risk already cited as a driver of quarterly revenue swings [02_business-identity.md §3a; `10_external-dependency.md`, Weather row]. | 50 |

Four of ten sources show real, evidenced advantage (cost advantage, natural resource access, licenses/regulation, location advantage), with brand adding a small, real but currently unquantified edge. The strongest two — cost advantage and natural resource access — are mechanically linked: captive bauxite and captive/contracted hydropower are what produce the 16th-percentile cost-curve position. This is a genuine advantage over the three named competitors in the *upstream* chain (Bauxite & Alumina, Aluminium Metal, Energy); it does **not** extend to Metal Markets or Hydro Extrusions, where no moat source in this table is evidenced (see §3-5).

## 3. Competitive Economics

| Company / Competitor | Gross Margin | EBIT Margin | Return on capital (ROIC, or ROE for financials) | Period | Source |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|---|
| Norsk Hydro (NHY) | 35.3% | 18.5% | Adjusted RoaCE 10.2% (FY2025); Reported (unadjusted) RoaCE 7.2% (FY2025); 5-yr average Adjusted RoaCE 13.3% (FY2021-2025) | LTM as of 2026-07-18 (margins); FY2025 / 5-yr (RoaCE) | Company Comparable Analysis Norsk Hydro ASA.xls, Operating Statistics tab, as of 2026-07-18 (margins); integrated-annual-report-2025.pdf, Alternative Performance Measures, p.234 and p.1563 (RoaCE) |
| Competitor A — RUSAL (SEHK:486) | 17.3% | 2.9% | ROE ~6.9% — dated, unverified web read, not RUSAL's own filing | LTM as of 2026-07-18 (margins); recent period, unverified (ROE) | Company Comparable Analysis Norsk Hydro ASA.xls, Operating Statistics tab, as of 2026-07-18 (margins); `08_competitive-map.md` citing Web: wisesheets.io ROE page, accessed 2026-07-19 (unverified) |
| Competitor B — Chalco (SEHK:2600) | 20.2% | 14.7% | ROE ~18.6%, ROIC ~10.1% — dated, unverified web read, not Chalco's own filing | LTM as of 2026-07-18 (margins); recent period, unverified (ROE/ROIC) | Company Comparable Analysis Norsk Hydro ASA.xls, Operating Statistics tab, as of 2026-07-18 (margins); `08_competitive-map.md` citing Web: search aggregation citing Chalco metrics, accessed 2026-07-19 (unverified) |
| Competitor C — Hindalco (BSE:500440) | 30.7% | 9.9% | ROCE ~14.6%, ROE ~13.9% — dated, unverified web read, not Hindalco's own filing | LTM as of 2026-07-18 (margins); FY2025, unverified (ROCE/ROE) | Company Comparable Analysis Norsk Hydro ASA.xls, Operating Statistics tab, as of 2026-07-18 (margins); `08_competitive-map.md` citing Web: alphaspread.com / gurufocus.com Hindalco ratio pages, accessed 2026-07-19 (unverified) |

**The economic moat test.** Return on capital sits **above** cost of capital on Hydro's own 5-year through-cycle basis, but only **at / marginally above** it on the latest-year and unadjusted bases:

> Return on capital **above** cost of capital on the 5-year through-cycle basis: **13.3% 5-yr average Adjusted RoaCE (FY2021-2025)** vs **10% "over-the-cycle" target**, +330bps [integrated-annual-report-2025.pdf, Alternative Performance Measures, p.234: "Over the last 5 years, the average adjusted RoaCE is 13.3 percent... above the target of 10 percent over the cycle"]. On the latest single year and on an unadjusted basis, the gap nearly disappears: FY2025 Adjusted RoaCE 10.2% vs the 10% target (+20bps only), and FY2025 **Reported** (unadjusted) RoaCE is 7.2% — **below** the 10% target [integrated-annual-report-2025.pdf, p.234, "Reported / Adjusted" RoaCE table].

Notes on this test:
- **Cost-of-capital source.** Hydro does not disclose a single group WACC figure. The best available company-disclosed anchor is its own stated strategic target, "Adjusted RoaCE > 10 percent over-the-cycle," which management explicitly frames as calibrated to differentiated business-area cost of capital ("Cost of capital and ARoaCE targets are differentiated for each business area... due to industry cyclicality") [integrated-annual-report-2025.pdf, p.1006-1007]. As corroborating (not primary) context, Hydro separately discloses a pre-tax nominal WACC range of 9.25%-11.75% (FY2025) used for goodwill/asset impairment testing, differentiated by asset [integrated-annual-report-2025.pdf, Note on impairment testing, p.162]. Converting this pre-tax range to post-tax terms at Hydro's own 30% standardized adjustment tax rate implies roughly 6.5%-8.2% post-tax — *Inference, not from filings* — which brackets the 10% target from below and is broadly consistent with using 10% as the working cost-of-capital proxy.
- **Segment split matters more than the group number.** Hydro's own FY2025 disclosure states plainly: "Energy and the upstream business areas delivered returns well above their cost of capital... The downstream segments delivered ARoaCE below their cost of capital" [integrated-annual-report-2025.pdf, p.1559-1562]. FY2025 Adjusted RoaCE by segment: Bauxite & Alumina 18.6%, Energy 17.2%, Aluminium Metal 14.4%, Metal Markets 0.8%, Extrusions -2.2% [integrated-annual-report-2025.pdf, p.1552-1570 chart]. The group's above-cost-of-capital read is entirely carried by the upstream/Energy chain where the natural-resource-access and cost-advantage moat sources actually sit (§2); Metal Markets and Extrusions — the two segments with no evidenced moat source — sit below cost of capital.
- **Management-headline cross-check.** Hydro's own Reported (unadjusted, actual-tax) RoaCE (7.2%, FY2025) is materially lower than its Adjusted RoaCE (10.2%, FY2025) — the adjusted figure strips out items including a NOK 1,504m unrealized LME-related loss, NOK 1,795m rationalization/closure charges and NOK 1,069m impairment charges [integrated-annual-report-2025.pdf, p.1546-1551]. Per source hierarchy, the more conservative Reported figure is flagged here rather than silently accepting the higher Adjusted headline; the 5-year through-cycle Adjusted average (13.3%) is used for the primary verdict because it is the best available multi-year, cycle-spanning figure disclosed, but the single-year Reported figure (7.2%, below the 10% proxy) is a live caveat, not a rounding footnote.
- **Vendor figure not preferred.** Capital IQ's own standardized "Return on Capital %" for Hydro is higher still — 18.0% (FY2025), 5-yr range 16.1%-24.6% [Norsk Hydro ASA OB NHY Financials.xls, Ratios tab] — but this uses a different EBIT definition (CIQ's "Operating Income" of NOK 41,218m for FY2025 does not reconcile to Hydro's own segment-note reported EBIT of NOK 14,401m [`03_segment-map.md` §2], a NOK ~27bn gap this pool cannot fully explain from available detail) and a capital base not verified against Hydro's own Capital Employed figure. This vendor figure is **not preferred** for the economic-moat test; Hydro's own audited-report RoaCE figures are used instead, consistent with the source hierarchy (company filing over vendor export for the same metric).
- **Normalized tax rate.** Hydro's own Adjusted net income methodology tax-effects one-off adjusting items (unrealized LME losses, impairments, rationalization charges) at a standardized 30 percent rate rather than the distorted actual effective tax rate, which swung from 24.3% (2021) to 57.2% (2023) to 39.5% (2025) [Norsk Hydro ASA OB NHY Financials.xls, Income Statement tab; integrated-annual-report-2025.pdf, Note on adjusted net income, p.10317]. This report uses that same 30% standardized rate as the anchor for any normalized NOPAT read, for consistency with `valuation/04_intrinsic-dcf` where that module runs.
- **Net-cash check.** Not applicable — Hydro carries net debt, not net cash (Net Debt/EBITDA 0.24x-0.35x, FY2021-FY2025; cash NOK 16,085m vs total debt NOK 36,574m, FY2025) [Norsk-Hydro-ASA-OB-NHY-Financials, Ratios tab and Balance Sheet tab], so no gross-vs-net-of-cash capital-base adjustment is required.

## 4. Where The Company Sits

1. **Relative to peers:** Hydro sits at the **top** of the named peer set on margin — LTM EBITDA margin 23.7% vs Chalco 18.6%, Hindalco 12.9% and RUSAL 7.0% [`08_competitive-map.md` §3] — but the peer return-on-capital figures are dated, unverified web reads (not each peer's own primary filing), so a precise ranking on return on capital cannot be made with confidence; on the numbers as reported, Hindalco's cited ROCE (~14.6%) and Chalco's cited ROE (~18.6%) may exceed Hydro's own FY2025 Adjusted RoaCE (10.2%), though these are not apples-to-apples metrics (ROCE/ROE vs RoaCE) [`08_competitive-map.md`, Competitor C].
2. **Absolute (the economic moat test):** the company earns a return on capital **above** its cost-of-capital proxy on a 5-year through-cycle basis (13.3% vs 10%) but only **at/marginally above** it on the latest year (10.2% Adjusted vs 10%) and **below** it on the latest year's unadjusted/Reported basis (7.2% vs 10%) — see §3 for the full breakdown and the segment split that explains the gap.

## 5. Moat Verdict

**Narrow moat.** The strongest, best-evidenced advantage is **cost advantage / natural resource access**, combined score reflecting captive bauxite (Paragominas, ~100% of two smelter/refinery chains) and captive/long-contract hydropower, which place Hydro's primary smelting at the 16th percentile of the global cost curve — genuinely hard for RUSAL, Chalco or Hindalco to replicate without owning equivalent captive resources. But the hard rule applies here: the group's return on capital sits only modestly above its cost-of-capital proxy through the cycle (13.3% vs 10%, +330bps) and is at or below it on the latest year depending on which return figure (Adjusted vs Reported) is used — this is not the clear, durable margin the "Strong moat" bar requires, and it is entirely carried by the upstream/Energy segments while Metal Markets and Extrusions sit below cost of capital with no evidenced moat source of their own. The durability test over the next 5 years: can the 16th-percentile cost position and captive-resource base be defended as Chinese and Russian-linked producers (Chalco, Hongqiao, RUSAL) expand or as Norwegian hydropower concessions approach their ~2050 reversion point, while Extrusions either stabilizes or continues shedding capacity. Industry rate-of-change scored 68/100 in `07_business-quality.md` (above the ≤40 fast-changing threshold), so no additional disruption-based durability discount applies — this is a slow-moving, capital-cycle industry, not a technology-cycle bet.

**Moat trajectory: eroding.** At the whole-company level the trajectory points down, not sideways: Hydro Extrusions' EBIT margin fell from ~4% (2020-2023) to -2.2% (2025), triggering five proposed European plant closures [`03_segment-map.md`, Extrusions row] — a segment losing, not gaining, competitive ground. The upstream cost-curve position (16th percentile) has no disclosed multi-year trend in this pool to confirm it is widening, and `07_business-quality.md`'s competitive-intensity row (score 45/100) flags that "a mid-cost-curve competitor a few years from now is a live possibility, not a tail risk" given global overcapacity dynamics — a stable-to-slightly-eroding read for the segment that actually carries the moat. Combined, the group-level trajectory is judged eroding, driven by the downstream segment's real, evidenced decline and a caution flag (not yet a trend) on the upstream cost position.

# External Dependency Check — NHY

## 1. Dependency Table

| External Variable | Dependency Level (Low / Mid / High) | Why It Matters | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Commodity prices (aluminium, alumina) | High | Hydro is an integrated aluminium producer — bauxite, alumina, primary metal, and extrusions. Realized aluminium price (LME) was USD 2,573/mt in FY2025 vs USD 2,374/mt in FY2024 and USD 2,218/mt in FY2023 — a direct swing factor in reported earnings, not a one-off. The 3-month LME price jumped from USD 2,995/mt to above USD 3,400/mt within a single quarter (Q1 2026) on a supply shock. The majority of alumina Hydro sells externally is contractually linked "to either the LME prices or alumina index with one-month delay," so alumina revenue is also a derivative of the aluminium price. | [FY2025 Annual Report, p.37 (Key financial data table)]; [Q1 FY2026 transcript, Apr-29-2026, prepared remarks, p.4-5: "The 3-month aluminum price began the quarter at $2,995 per tonne and finished above $3,400 per tonne"]; [FY2025 Annual Report, p.37, footnote 4 to Key financial data] |
| Interest rates | Low | Disclosed sensitivity to a 10% rate increase is small: NOK 65m on derivative financial instruments and NOK 7m on other financial instruments, versus FY2025 Adjusted EBITDA of NOK 28,889m — under 0.3% of EBITDA. | [FY2025 Annual Report, Note 8.2 Financial instruments, Sensitivity analysis table, p.193] |
| FX (USD/NOK, EUR, BRL) | High | Hydro's revenue is priced in USD (LME) while its main cost base — labor, most power contracts, and capex — is in NOK, creating a structural currency mismatch. Company-disclosed sensitivity: a NOK 1.00 move in USD/NOK (roughly a 10% move off the FY2025 realized rate of 10.39) swings Adjusted EBITDA by NOK 4,900 million, equal to ~17% of FY2025 Adjusted EBITDA of NOK 28,889m. BRL and EUR moves also swing results and financial-item revaluations materially. | [FY2025 Annual Report, p.38, "Key financial exposures" currency-sensitivity table: "Sustainable effect, Adj. EBITDA" row, USD column NOK 4,900m]; [FY2025 Annual Report, p.37, "Realized USD/NOK exchange rate 10.39"] |
| Freight / logistics rates | Mid | Regional aluminium premiums Hydro realizes (e.g., the US-Europe "Atlantic differential") move with shipping costs, not just metal supply/demand. Management attributed a Q1 2026 narrowing of this differential directly to "higher oil prices driving up shipping costs," on top of a Middle East conflict already disrupting trade flows. | [Q1 FY2026 transcript, Apr-29-2026, prepared remarks, p.4: "The Atlantic differential did decrease... this is primarily caused by higher oil prices driving up shipping costs"] |
| Government policy (trade/tariffs) | High | US Section 232 tariffs (a 50% import duty) directly lifted the US Midwest aluminium premium Hydro realizes from "just over $2,000 per tonne at the end of '25 to north of $2,500" by end-Q1 2026 — a policy-driven price move, not a market one. EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) enters its definitive phase from January 2026 and is being revised/expanded through 2034, changing the competitive playing field for Hydro's EU-facing production. | [Q1 FY2026 transcript, Apr-29-2026, prepared remarks, p.4-5]; [FY2025 Annual Report, Risk Review, p.52: "CBAM is expected to be revised several times between 2026 and 2034... entry into definitive phase in January 2026"] |
| Regulation (carbon / EU ETS) | High | Free EU ETS carbon-allowance allocation for aluminium production is being phased out between 2026 and 2034, turning CO2 into "a variable operational cost at plant level," and Hydro explicitly builds a house view of the carbon price into its planning. Norway's Indirect Carbon Cost (ICC) compensation scheme (valid 2024-2030) offsets part of this, but only through 2030 and only in Norway. | [FY2025 Annual Report, p.52 (Risk Review, Regulatory and policy framework uncertainty): "the free allocation of ETS allowances for aluminium production will be gradually phased out between 2026 to 2034"]; [FY2025 Annual Report, Note on climate/EU ETS, referencing "Hydro uses the EU ETS carbon price in a carbon price in Hydro's analysis, costs related to CO2 emissions become a variable operational cost"] |
| Weather | Mid/High | Roughly half of Hydro Energy's ~18 TWh/year Nordic power portfolio is captive hydropower (9.4 TWh in a normal year), and hydropower output is "strongly influenced by hydrological conditions," with "volatility in both production as well as electricity spot prices" causing "significant variations in quarterly revenues." In Brazil, power prices "rose rapidly in March to remain at a high level throughout the year due to persistently weak hydrology" in 2025, raising smelter input costs there. Weather-driven power-price uncertainty was cited as a reason Hydro fully wrote down its Tomago (Australia) smelter: "the full write-down reflects the significant uncertainty regarding future power prices beyond the current power price agreements expiring in 2028." | [FY2025 Annual Report, p.15 (Business Areas — Energy): "Hydro Energy owns captive power production at 9.4 TWh... total power portfolio to 18 TWh per year"; "Volatility in both production as well as electricity spot prices may however cause significant variations in quarterly revenues"]; [FY2025 Annual Report, p.26 (Market development, Energy): "prices in the Brazilian power market... rose rapidly in March to remain at a high level throughout the year due to persistently weak hydrology"]; [FY2025 Annual Report, Notes, impairment discussion: "the full write-down reflects the significant uncertainty regarding future power prices beyond the current power price agreements expiring in 2028"] |
| Geopolitics | High | A Middle East conflict and closure of the Strait of Hormuz was the stated cause of the Q1 2026 aluminium price spike: the region supplies "some 9% of global output" and exports "4 million to 5 million tonnes... annually," and "the combination of the announced curtailments in the region and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz severely impacts global metal supply," with the resulting undersupply pushing the 3-month LME price from USD 2,995/mt to above USD 3,400/mt in one quarter. Persistent discounted Russian metal flows into the market via China (SHFE) were also cited as holding down realized prices in FY2025. | [Q1 FY2026 transcript, Apr-29-2026, prepared remarks, p.4]; [FY2025 Annual Report, p.26 (Market development): "Chinese SHFE prices were higher than LME throughout the year even with a constant inflow of Russian metal at discounted prices"] |
| Consumer cycle | Mid | Hydro Extrusions sells into construction, automotive, and durable-goods end markets that track the consumer/economic cycle. Management's own framing: "The aluminium industry is pro-cyclical with demand for products closely linked to overall economic conditions." European extrusion full-year demand growth for 2026 was cut to "around 1%" during the quarter. | [FY2025 Annual Report, Risk Review, p.49: "The aluminium industry is pro-cyclical with demand for products closely linked to overall economic conditions"]; [Q1 FY2026 transcript, Apr-29-2026, prepared remarks, p.5: "Full year growth is now expected at around 1%"] |
| Industrial cycle | High | Primary aluminium demand, Extrusions volumes, and Metal Markets/recycling margins are all tied to global industrial and automotive/building demand; overcapacity in a downturn has already forced a curtailment decision (the Slovalco smelter in Slovakia is "currently curtailed"), and management has cut workforce and investment levels in response to "macroeconomic uncertainty and weak markets" during 2025. | [FY2025 Annual Report, p.15 (Business Areas — Aluminium Metal): "five partly owned smelters in Qatar, Brazil, Canada, Australia, and Slovakia (currently curtailed)"]; [FY2025 Annual Report, Risk Review, p.49: "Hydro has taken measures during the course of 2025 to ensure its financial flexibility including a diligent cost focus, reduction in overall workforce, and cuts in investment levels"] |

## 2. Sensitivity, If Disclosed

Hydro publishes its own commodity and currency sensitivities in the FY2025 Annual Report ("Key financial exposures," p.38, supplementing the IFRS-required disclosure in Note 8.2). These are net-of-hedge, annual sensitivities based on normal production volumes as of 31 December 2025.

| Variable | Move | Effect on Adjusted EBITDA (NOK million) | Citation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Aluminium price | +USD 10/mt | +150 | [FY2025 Annual Report, p.38, "Commodity price sensitivity +10 USD/mt"] |
| USD/NOK | +1.00 NOK/USD (weaker NOK) | +4,900 (sustainable effect) | [FY2025 Annual Report, p.38, currency-sensitivity table] |
| USD/NOK | (same move) | (680) one-off revaluation effect on financial items | [FY2025 Annual Report, p.38] |
| BRL/NOK | +0.10 NOK/BRL | (520) sustainable effect / +480 one-off revaluation | [FY2025 Annual Report, p.38] |
| EUR/NOK | +1.00 NOK/EUR | (210) sustainable effect / (3,310) one-off revaluation | [FY2025 Annual Report, p.38] |

A separate IFRS-mandated table (Note 8.2) shows a hypothetical 10% price/rate move applied to derivative and other financial instruments held at year-end only (it excludes offsetting physical positions): a 10% increase in commodity (aluminium) prices would produce a NOK 3,487m loss on derivative commodity instruments at 31-Dec-2025, and a 10% increase in USD/NOK would produce a combined loss of roughly NOK 1,500m across derivative and other financial instruments — these are point-in-time, instruments-only figures and are not directly comparable to the "Key financial exposures" table above, which nets in the operating exposure. [FY2025 Annual Report, Note 8.2, Sensitivity analysis, p.193]

## 3. Classification

**Mostly externally driven.** Hydro's earnings move first and most on the LME aluminium price, the alumina price/index it is contractually tied to, the USD/NOK exchange rate, power prices, EU carbon policy, and — as Q1 2026 showed in real time — geopolitical supply shocks and US tariff policy. Management's levers are real but narrow: forward hedging on the LME (up to about three years), NOK-denominated debt to partly match the cost base, a lower-cost position on the industry cost curve, a higher mix of value-add/recycled product versus standard ingot, and operational flexibility (curtailment) in a downturn. None of these levers changes the direction of the LME price, the carbon price, or a currency move — they only cushion the size of the swing.

## 4. External Dependency Risk Score

**74/100** (this score is INVERTED — higher = worse / more dangerous external dependence).

Rationale: the FX sensitivity alone (NOK 4,900m per NOK 1.00 move, ~17% of FY2025 Adjusted EBITDA) and the commodity/geopolitics evidence (a single quarter's LME move of over USD 400/mt driven by a Middle East supply shock) show that quarter-to-quarter results are dominated by variables management does not set. The score sits in the 61-80 "mostly externally driven, limited management levers" band rather than the 81-100 "pure pass-through" band because Hydro does have a genuine, evidenced cost-curve advantage (competitive, partly self-generated hydropower) and an active hedging program that measurably dampens — though does not eliminate — the swings.

## 5. The Single Biggest Lever

The USD/NOK exchange rate: Hydro's revenue is set in US dollars (LME-linked) while its dominant cost base is in Norwegian kroner, and the company's own disclosed sensitivity — NOK 4,900 million of Adjusted EBITDA per NOK 1.00 move in USD/NOK — implies that a 20% adverse move (a materially stronger NOK, roughly NOK 2.00 off the FY2025 realized rate of 10.39) would swing Adjusted EBITDA by close to NOK 9.8 billion, more than a third of FY2025 Adjusted EBITDA of NOK 28,889m, on a factor Hydro cannot control and only partially hedges through the currency of its debt [FY2025 Annual Report, p.38, "Key financial exposures"].

| Off-balance-sheet items | Contingent liabilities are material and not fully quantifiable: known tax disputes (mostly Brazilian indirect tax) total ~NOK 4.3bn, of which ~NOK 3.6bn is considered a possible loss (partly covered by acquisition-related tax indemnities), plus open Alunorte-related litigation in Brazil and the Netherlands (Cainquiama Rotterdam case dismissed Sep-2025 but appealed Dec-2025; multiple Pará collective-action and criminal cases still pending) where the company states it cannot estimate a range of outcomes. | [FY2025 Annual Report, Note (Provisions/Contingent liabilities), p.7801-7840 ("known cases amount to about NOK 4.3 billion, of which losses are considered possible in cases amounting to about NOK 3.6 billion"); ESG Factbook, p.12022-12075 (Cainquiama Rotterdam case dismissed then appealed; Pará collective actions and criminal case pending)] | 45 |
| Working capital trend (receivable days, inventory days, cash conversion) | Days-sales-outstanding held in the 30-39 day range through FY2021-FY2025 before jumping to 56.7 days on an LTM (Mar-2026) basis, matched by accounts receivable roughly doubling quarter-on-quarter from NOK 17,212m (Dec-2025) to NOK 31,384m (Mar-2026); days-inventory-out stayed a tighter, roughly stable 74-85 days across the period. | [Capital IQ Ratios export: "Avg. Days Sales Out." 39.3/30.4/32.1/33.1/33.0/56.7 for FY2021-FY2025 and LTM Mar-2026; "Avg. Days Inventory Out." 84.8/73.1/82.0/75.9/76.8/77.1 same periods; Balance Sheet export, Accounts Receivable NOK 17,212m (Dec-2025) vs NOK 31,384m (Mar-2026)] | 40 |
| Senior management turnover (CEO, CFO, board chair in last 3 years) | The CEO (Eivind Kallevik, Hydro employee since 1998) and CFO (Trond Olaf Christophersen, Hydro employee since 1997) both moved into their current roles in 2024, and the Board Chair (Rune Bjerke, a director since 2020) became Chair in May 2024 after serving as Deputy Chair — a coordinated leadership transition, but all three are long-tenured internal promotions rather than external hires or departures under pressure. | [FY2025 Annual Report, "Other details" table, p.2045-2046 (Kallevik "Employed in Hydro since 1998... Position since 2024"; Christophersen "since 1997... Position since 2024"); Board Members export (Bjerke: "Chair since May 07, 2024", director since 2020)] | 30 |

## 2. Classification

**Standard professional management.**

No row scores in the high-severity range for a hard governance flag (auditor, restatements, pledging, ownership are all clean or not applicable), and the acquisition pattern does not meet the serial-acquirer bar — one bolt-on deal in five years plus active divestment of non-core bets is portfolio discipline, not empire-building. At the same time this is not a clean "owner-operator" profile: capex has run consistently above depreciation, the Q1 2026 working-capital jump is unexplained in the pool, and Hydro carries real, only partly quantified, off-balance-sheet exposure (Brazilian tax disputes and Alunorte litigation) that a pure discipline read would not have. The combination is a professionally run, state-anchored industrial company with ordinary-course capital allocation and a handful of items — contingent liabilities and the receivable spike — that warrant monitoring rather than alarm.

## 3. Most Material Signal

The off-balance-sheet contingent liabilities row is the one that would change the classification if it deteriorated. Hydro's own filing puts ~NOK 3.6bn of Brazilian tax exposure at "possible" loss and states it "is not possible... to provide a range of possible outcomes" for the Alunorte litigation, which spans a dismissed-then-appealed Rotterdam case and multiple pending Pará collective and criminal actions [FY2025 Annual Report, p.7801-7840, p.12022-12075]. None of this is provisioned beyond existing balance-sheet amounts, so an adverse ruling — particularly the appealed criminal penalty or a reversal on appeal in the Rotterdam case — could convert a currently unquantified contingency into a cash outflow with no advance warning in the numbers reviewed here. That is the one item that could push this from "standard professional management" toward "governance red flags" if it worsens.

## 4. Capital Allocation Score /100

**62/100.**

No rejector-filter cap applies: the acquisition-pattern row scored 25/100 severity, well below the ≥70 threshold that would trigger the Filter 4 cap (CLAUDE.md §24, Filter 4) — Hydro's M&A record over the review period is one bolt-on acquisition plus voluntary divestment of non-core bets, not a serial-acquirer pattern. The score of 62 reflects clean share-count, dividend, debt, auditor and ownership signals pulled down by the two moderate-to-high severity rows that are genuinely unresolved in the data: the unquantified Brazilian tax/Alunorte contingent liabilities (45 severity) and the unexplained Q1 2026 receivable-days spike (40 severity), plus above-depreciation capex (35) and a same-year CEO/CFO/Chair transition (30) that, while internally sourced, concentrates leadership change in one year.

Contingent liabilities and receivable trend are quoted directly from the filing in the company's own home currency (NOK); no translation issue arose since all reviewed documents are in English [FY2025 Annual Report, filing regime confirmed Norway/Oslo Børs, English-language filing].

# Red Flags Sweep — NHY

All source documents in this pool are in English (confirmed in `00_data-triage.md` §2A) — no language-related flags apply here (CLAUDE.md §27).

| external-dependency | USD/NOK currency mismatch (NOK 4,900m Adjusted EBITDA per NOK 1.00 move); commodity price/geopolitical supply-shock exposure; CBAM/EU ETS carbon-cost phase-out 2026-2034; hydrology/weather risk to captive hydropower and Brazil power costs; US tariff exposure |

## 2. New Red Flags

| Red Flag | Why It Matters | Evidence | Severity /100 *(higher = worse)* |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| Alumetal (2023 acquisition) sitting close to impairment | Hydro's own FY2025 impairment test found the Alumetal recycler group's recoverable amount (value-in-use) exceeds its NOK 2.7bn carrying value by only about 18% — a thin cushion — and the company states directly that "continued weak market conditions or further weakening of demand and/or margins is likely to result in impairment in a future period." This is a live, quantified, company-flagged risk on a deal only 2-3 years old, distinct from the already-covered Extrusions plant closures (which sit in a different segment, Extrusions vs. Metal Markets/recycling) | [integrated-annual-report-2025.pdf, Note 2.2 Impairment, p.163-164: "An impairment indicator was identified for Alumetal, a recycler group with a carrying value of NOK 2,7 billion, acquired in 2023, due to the weak market conditions for recycling. The impairment test concluded that the recoverable amount... exceeds the carrying amount of the CGU by about 18%, and no impairment was required in 2025. As the coverage is limited, continued weak market conditions or further weakening of demand and/or margins is likely to result in impairment in a future period."] | 55 |
| Cybersecurity / OT risk trending up, not yet tested by a disclosed breach | Hydro's own enterprise risk review classifies "Major breach of cyber security" as a Business risk with a rising trend arrow, explicitly citing that industrial control systems at mine, refinery, smelter, and hydropower sites are exposed and that "several high profile manufacturing companies have experienced significant breaches in 2025." A breach of process-control systems (not just IT) at a physically continuous, capital-intensive production process (smelting, refining) can cause direct operational/safety disruption, not just a data-privacy event. No breach has occurred per the pool, and mitigations are disclosed, but the risk itself is untested and rising | [integrated-annual-report-2025.pdf, Risk review, p.55: "MAJOR BREACH OF CYBER SECURITY... Ability to influence: Moderate, Trend: ↗ (increased uncertainty)"; "the underlying cyber security risk to industrial control systems continues to be sustained at a high level... several high profile manufacturing companies have experienced significant breaches in 2025"] | 35 |
| Unexplained 55.7% YoY jump in Norway (home-market) revenue | Norway revenue rose from NOK 7,831m (FY2024) to NOK 12,190m (FY2025), a 55.7% jump versus low-single-digit or negative growth in every other major geography that year. No explanation for this specific jump appears anywhere in the pool (annual report, Q1 2026 report, transcripts, or investor decks); customer-geography flagged it as "not explained in the pool text" but out of scope for that agent to investigate. It could be a benign internal-trading/reclassification effect given Norway is also the production hub, but as reported it is an unexplained anomaly in an otherwise granular geographic revenue table | [integrated-annual-report-2025.pdf, Note 1.4, p.152 — Norway revenue NOK 12,190m (2025) vs NOK 7,831m (2024); flagged but not investigated in `05_customer-geography.md` §2] | 20 |

## 3. Most Severe New Flag

The most material new flag is the thin impairment headroom on the Alumetal recycler group: Hydro's own FY2025 test shows the recoverable amount clears the NOK 2.7bn carrying value by only about 18%, and management's own words say continued weak recycling-market conditions are "likely" to force an impairment in a future period. This is not a hypothetical stress scenario invented by this sweep — it is the company's stated forward view on an asset from its only material acquisition of the last five years (per `11_capital-allocation-governance.md`). The synthesizer should treat this as a near-term earnings and capital-allocation risk (a bolt-on deal already showing cracks), separate from — and additive to — the already-flagged Extrusions plant-closure impairments, because it sits in a different segment (Metal Markets/recycling) and reflects deal-specific execution risk rather than the broader European demand downturn.

## 4. Cross-Cutting Patterns

Impairment activity in FY2025 is broader than any single upstream report captures in one place: five Extrusions plants written down (NOK 397m) plus two further Extrusions CGUs in the UK and France (NOK 192m + NOK 96m) on weak European demand, a hydrogen-technology impairment (NOK 265m) tied to the already-noted de-prioritization of renewables, and now the Alumetal indicator sitting at only 18% headroom — four distinct impairment events across three different segments (Extrusions, Energy, Metal Markets) in the same fiscal year, on top of the already fully written-down Tomago smelter. Individually each is disclosed and modest in size, but together they describe a business currently absorbing write-downs across most of its downstream and diversification bets simultaneously, while the upstream segments (Bauxite & Alumina, Aluminium Metal) carry the group's profit. That pattern — upstream commodity segments funding a downstream/diversification book that is currently shedding value — is consistent with, and reinforces, the segment-rotation dynamic already identified in `03_segment-map.md` and the weak-pricing-power read in `07_business-quality.md`.
